title: SQL for Product Questions
tagline: Answer your own questions without waiting for the data team.
summary: A practical first course in SQL for product managers, designers and anyone who keeps asking analysts for numbers.
description:
Most product questions are small: how many teams used the new export last week, which plan churns fastest, where people drop out of onboarding. This course teaches you just enough SQL to answer them yourself, using one realistic product database from start to finish.

You will write every query by hand. By the end you will be comfortable with filters, joins, grouping and simple funnels, and you will know when a question really does need an analyst.
outcomes:
Read a product database and understand how its tables connect
Filter, sort and count with SELECT, WHERE and GROUP BY
Join users, accounts and events without double counting
Build a simple activation funnel
Know when a number is trustworthy and when to ask for help

title: Dashboards People Actually Use
summary: Design dashboards around the decisions people make, choose the right chart for each question, and keep them trusted over time.
description:
Most dashboards are built once and ignored forever. This course starts from the decisions a team makes every week and works backwards to the few numbers that support them.

You will redesign a cluttered dashboard step by step, learn which chart types answer which questions, and set up the habits that keep a dashboard honest after launch.
outcomes:
Start every dashboard from a decision, not a data source
Pick chart types that match the question
Use layout and colour to direct attention
Write definitions so numbers mean the same thing to everyone
Retire dashboards nobody uses

title: Design Systems from Scratch
tagline: Build the foundations before the components.
summary: Plan, build and document a small design system that a real product team will actually adopt.
description:
A design system is a product with designers and engineers as its users. This course walks through building one for a small team: auditing what exists, choosing tokens, building the first components and writing documentation people read.

The focus is on decisions and adoption rather than tools, so it works whether your team uses Figma, code-first components or both.
outcomes:
Audit an existing interface and find the real inconsistencies
Define colour, type and spacing tokens
Build components with clear states and variants
Write documentation that answers real questions
Plan adoption and versioning

title: Interface Typography
tagline: Type that reads well on every screen.
summary: A focused course on choosing, sizing and pairing type for product interfaces and marketing pages.
description: Typography does most of the work in an interface, yet it is often chosen last. This course covers the practical side: picking typefaces that hold up at small sizes, building a type scale, setting line length and spacing, and pairing fonts with restraint.
outcomes:
Choose typefaces that work at interface sizes
Build a modular type scale
Set comfortable line length and line height
Pair two typefaces with confidence

title: Product Discovery in Practice
tagline: Learn what to build before you build it.
summary: Interview customers, map opportunities and test ideas cheaply, so your team ships things people need.
description: Discovery is the work of reducing risk before you commit engineering time. This course covers the habits that make it routine: weekly customer conversations, opportunity mapping, and small experiments that test the riskiest assumption first.
outcomes:
Run customer interviews that reveal real behaviour
Map opportunities and choose where to focus
Find the riskiest assumption in an idea
Design small, fast experiments
Share discovery so the whole team learns

title: Writing Clear Product Specs
tagline: Short documents that align the whole team.
summary: Write product specs that explain the problem, the decision and the plan in a way engineers and stakeholders actually read.
description: A good spec is a thinking tool and a communication tool. This course shows a simple structure for one-page specs, how to write about problems before solutions, and how to keep specs alive as plans change.
outcomes:
Structure a one-page spec
Describe problems with evidence
Write clear scope and non-goals
Keep specs current as work changes

title: Leading Your First Team
tagline: The first ninety days as a new manager.
summary: One-to-ones, feedback, delegation and meetings: the core habits for people who have just become managers.
description:
Becoming a manager changes your job overnight, but nobody hands you a manual. This course covers the habits that matter most in the first ninety days: getting to know your team, running useful one-to-ones, giving feedback, delegating and keeping meetings short.

It is practical and honest about the awkward parts, with exercises you can use with your team the same week.
outcomes:
Plan your first ninety days
Run one-to-ones that build trust
Give feedback that is specific and kind
Delegate outcomes rather than tasks
Run meetings people find useful
